title: Power Markets & Market Design
description: Merit order, marginal pricing, the day-ahead/intraday/balancing timeline, spreads, PPAs and negative prices.

cards.back: Generators ranked by **short-run marginal cost**, cheapest first. The market dispatches up the stack until supply meets demand; the last unit needed sets the price.

cards.front: Under *marginal (pay-as-clear) pricing*, what does a wind farm that bid €0 earn?
cards.back: The **clearing price** set by the marginal unit — not its own €0 bid. Everyone who clears is paid the same price; the gap over the plant's own cost is its **inframarginal rent**.

cards.front: Name the four stages of the electricity market timeline, earliest to latest.
cards.back: 1) **Forward / futures** (hedging, years–days ahead) → 2) **Day-ahead** auction → 3) **Intraday** (continuous, correct forecast errors) → 4) **Balancing** (TSO, real time).

cards.front: Why does electricity need a *sequence* of markets rather than one price?
cards.back: Power can barely be stored and supply must match demand every instant. Each successive market lets participants re-balance as forecasts (especially wind/solar) sharpen toward delivery.

cards.front: In a renewables-heavy hour, what most directly sets whether the price is high, low, or negative?
cards.back: The dispatchable fleet and the price respond to **residual (net) load**. When it falls toward zero, the marginal unit moves left and prices drop — sometimes below zero.

When inflexible **must-run** and subsidised output exceeds demand, it can be cheaper to *pay* to keep generating than to shut down and restart. A signal that flexibility (storage, interconnection, flexible demand) is scarce.

cards.front: What is the *spark spread*, and why does its sign matter?
cards.back: A gas plant's gross margin per MWh: $SS = P_{el} - P_{gas}/\eta$. A positive spread means running is profitable; the sign flips a plant in or out of the merit order.

cards.front: What does the *clean* spark spread add, and what does it reveal vs the clean dark spread?
cards.back: It subtracts the CO$_2$ cost: $CSS = P_{el} - P_{gas}/\eta - (e_{gas}/\eta)P_{CO_2}$. When a rising carbon price lifts the clean spark spread above the clean *dark* (coal) spread, gas undercuts coal — fuel switching that cuts emissions.

cards.front: Two adjacent bidding zones normally share one price. When do their prices *split*?
choices: When the interconnector between them congests (hits its capacity limit)
Whenever demand rises in either zone
When both zones use the same fuel
cards.back: Market coupling equalises prices as long as the link has spare capacity. Once it **congests**, cheap power can't fully reach the expensive zone and prices diverge.

cards.front: What does a *capacity market* pay for, and why add it to an energy-only market?
cards.back: It pays generators/demand-response to **be available** at peak, securing resource adequacy that energy-only prices may under-reward (the 'missing money' problem). The energy-only alternative is **scarcity pricing**.

cards.front: Gas plant: power price €70/MWh, gas €24/MWh$_{th}$, efficiency $\eta = 0.40$. Find the spark spread, €/MWh.
cards.back: $SS = 70 - 24/0.40 = 70 - 60 = 10$ €/MWh. (Divide the fuel price by efficiency first!)

cards.front: The day-ahead auction clears at €55/MWh, set by a gas peaker. A wind farm with ~€0 SRMC clears too. What inframarginal rent (€/MWh) does the wind farm earn?
cards.back: Rent $= P_{clear} - SRMC = 55 - 0 = 55$ €/MWh. Under pay-as-clear it is paid the full clearing price, leaving €55/MWh to cover fixed/capital costs.
